source.text: וּבֶן־הֲדַ֣ד מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֗ם קָבַץ֙ אֶת־כָּל־חֵיל֔וֹ וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים וּשְׁנַ֥יִם מֶ֛לֶךְ אִתּ֖וֹ וְס֣וּס וָרָ֑כֶב וַיַּ֗עַל וַיָּ֨צַר֙ עַל־שֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן וַיִּלָּ֖חֶם בָּֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered all his army, and thirty and two kings [were] with him, and horse and chariotry; and he went up and besieged Samaria and fought against it.

en.L: And Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered all his army, and thirty-two kings [were] with him, and horses and chariots; and he went up and laid siege to Samaria and fought against it.
en.B: Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered his whole army. Thirty-two kings were with him, along with horses and chariots. He marched up, laid siege to Samaria, and attacked it.
en.R: Ben-hadad, the king of Aram, brought his whole army together. Thirty-two other kings came with him, with their horses and chariots. He went up to the city of Samaria, surrounded it, and attacked it.

decisions.choice: Ben-hadad king of Aram: the ruler of the Aramean kingdom of Damascus
decisions.reason: Aram was the kingdom north-east of Israel, with its capital at Damascus (verse 34; 11:24; 15:18). Ben-hadad means "son of Hadad", the storm god of the Arameans, and more than one king bore the name. Whether this is the Ben-hadad of 15:18-20 or a later king of the same name, the text does not say.

decisions.choice: thirty-two kings: rulers of small states who fought under Ben-hadad
decisions.reason: In this region a "king" could rule a single city or tribe. These rulers were bound to Ben-hadad as allies or subjects and brought their forces with him (verse 16). Verse 24 shows that they kept command of their own troops.

decisions.choice: Samaria: the capital of the northern kingdom
decisions.reason: Omri, Ahab's father, built Samaria on a hill he bought and made it his capital (16:24). Besieging it was an attack on the heart of the kingdom.

decisions.choice: other kings; with their horses; surrounded it
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the kings were others besides Ben-hadad and that the horses and chariots were their forces, and gives "besieged" in plain words.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֧ח מַלְאָכִ֛ים אֶל־אַחְאָ֥ב מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הָעִֽירָה׃

records.literal_gloss: And he sent messengers to Ahab king of Israel into the city,

en.L: And he sent messengers to Ahab king of Israel into the city,
en.B: He sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel,
en.R: He sent messengers into the city to Ahab, the king of Israel.

decisions.choice: the sentence runs on into verse 3
decisions.reason: The messengers are sent with the words that verse 3 gives. The Hebrew verse ends here, but the sentence continues; verse 3 begins "and he said to him".

decisions.choice: messengers: envoys who spoke in their king's name
decisions.reason: A king's messengers delivered his words as if he were speaking himself, so the message in verse 3 begins "Thus says Ben-hadad" and is spoken in his first person.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר בֶּן־הֲדַ֔דכַּסְפְּךָ֥ וּֽזְהָבְךָ֖ לִֽי־ה֑וּא וְנָשֶׁ֧יךָ וּבָנֶ֛יךָ הַטּוֹבִ֖ים לִי־הֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: and he said to him, Thus says Ben-hadad, Your silver and your gold [are] to me, it; and your wives and your sons, the good [ones], [are] to me, they.

en.L: and he said to him, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'Your silver and your gold [are] mine, and your wives and your sons, the best [of them], [are] mine.'"
en.B: and said to him, "Ben-hadad says this: 'Your silver and your gold are mine, and the best of your wives and {{gender:children|sons}} are mine as well.'"
en.R: They told him, "This is what Ben-hadad says: 'Your silver and gold belong to me. The best of your wives and {{gender:children|sons}} are mine too.'"

decisions.choice: verse numbers: the Hebrew text begins verse 3 here
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. In the Hebrew text verse 2 ends with "into the city", and "And he said to him, Thus says Ben-hadad" opens verse 3. Many Bibles print those words at the end of verse 2 and begin verse 3 with "Your silver and your gold". The words are the same and the later verses keep the same numbers; only the place of the division differs.

decisions.choice: the best: the finest of his wives and sons
decisions.reason: "The good ones" follows both "your wives" and "your sons" and most likely limits them both: Ben-hadad claims the choicest of Ahab's household, as well as his silver and gold.

decisions.choice: are mine: a demand that Ahab become his subject
decisions.reason: Claiming a king's treasure and family was a demand for surrender. Ahab takes it as a claim of overlordship that he can accept with words and tribute (verse 4); verses 5-6 show that Ben-hadad means to take them in fact.

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: The word is "sons", but a king's offspring taken as hostages or plunder would include his daughters, so Balanced and Readable offer "children" with "sons" as the alternative.

decisions.choice: They told him
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "he said": Ben-hadad speaks through his messengers. Readable names the messengers as the speakers, since Ben-hadad himself is outside the city.

source.text: וַיַּ֤עַן מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וַיֹּ֔אמֶר כִּדְבָרְךָ֖ אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ לְךָ֥ אֲנִ֖י וְכָל־אֲשֶׁר־לִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered [the] king of Israel and said, According to your word, my lord the king; to you [am] I and all that [is] to me.

en.L: And the king of Israel answered and said, "As you say, my lord the king: I [am] yours, and all that I have."
en.B: The king of Israel answered, "It is as you say, my lord the king. I am yours, with all that I have."
en.R: The king of Israel answered, "You are right, my master the king. I belong to you, and so does everything I have."

decisions.choice: my lord the king: the words of a subject to his overlord
decisions.reason: Ahab speaks as a lesser king who accepts Ben-hadad as his master. By agreeing to the claim of verse 3 he is offering submission and tribute, in the hope of ending the siege.

decisions.choice: according to your word: I agree
decisions.reason: The phrase means "as you have said", a formal acceptance of the terms.

decisions.choice: my master the king
decisions.reason: Readable says "master" to make clear that "lord" here is a human overlord, not God.

source.text: וַיָּשֻׁ֨בוּ֙ הַמַּלְאָכִ֔ים וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֥ר בֶּן־הֲדַ֖ד לֵאמֹ֑ר כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֤חְתִּי אֵלֶ֨יךָ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר כַּסְפְּךָ֧ וּזְהָבְךָ֛ וְנָשֶׁ֥יךָ וּבָנֶ֖יךָ לִ֥י תִתֵּֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And returned the messengers and said, Thus says Ben-hadad, saying, Indeed I sent to you, saying, Your silver and your gold and your wives and your sons to me you will give,

en.L: And the messengers came back and said, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'I indeed sent to you, saying, "Your silver and your gold and your wives and your sons you shall give to me,"
en.B: The messengers came back and said, "Ben-hadad says this: 'I sent you word that you must hand over to me your silver and gold, your wives and your {{gender:children|sons}},
en.R: The messengers returned and said, "This is what Ben-hadad says: 'I sent you a message telling you to give me your silver and gold, your wives and your {{gender:children|sons}}.

decisions.choice: I indeed sent ... but tomorrow I will send: the second demand goes further than the first
alternatives: Although I sent to you ..., I will now send
decisions.reason: The words "I sent to you" recall the first message, and verse 6 goes on "but about this time tomorrow". Ben-hadad is not repeating himself: before, he claimed Ahab's goods; now he says his men will come and take them.

decisions.choice: you shall give: an order, not a request
decisions.reason: Ben-hadad restates his first message as a command. Ahab's polite answer in verse 4 has only made him bolder.

decisions.choice: I sent you word that you must hand over
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the quotation inside the quotation inside the quotation. Balanced and Readable give Ben-hadad's earlier message as reported speech, which is easier to follow.

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

source.text: כִּ֣י׀אִם־כָּעֵ֣ת מָחָ֗ר אֶשְׁלַ֤ח אֶת־עֲבָדַי֙ אֵלֶ֔יךָ וְחִפְּשׂוּ֙ אֶת־בֵּ֣יתְךָ֔ וְאֵ֖ת בָּתֵּ֣י עֲבָדֶ֑יךָ וְהָיָה֙ כָּל־מַחְמַ֣ד עֵינֶ֔יךָ יָשִׂ֥ימוּ בְיָדָ֖ם וְלָקָֽחוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: but about the time tomorrow I will send my servants to you, and they will search your house and [the] houses of your servants, and it will be [that] every desire of your eyes they will put in their hand and take [it].

en.L: but about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to you, and they will search your house and the houses of your servants, and every desire of your eyes they will put in their hand and take away.'"
en.B: but about this time tomorrow I will send my officials to you, and they will search your palace and the houses of your officials. They will lay their hands on everything you value and carry it off.'"
en.R: Now, at about this time tomorrow, I will send my officials to you. They will search your palace and the houses of your officials. They will grab everything you treasure and take it away.'"

decisions.choice: every desire of your eyes: everything you prize
decisions.reason: The phrase means whatever is precious and pleasing to someone (Ezekiel 24:16). Ben-hadad's men will take whatever Ahab values most.

decisions.choice: your eyes (the Hebrew text)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text reads "your eyes". The ancient Greek translation reads "their eyes", meaning whatever the searchers themselves like. Either way Ben-hadad's men will take what they choose.

decisions.choice: your house: the royal palace
decisions.reason: The house of a king is his palace, with its treasures and his household (verse 43; 9:1).

decisions.choice: put in their hand: seize
decisions.reason: To put something in one's hand is to take hold of it as one's own.

decisions.choice: servants (Literal); officials (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The servants of a king are his officials. Literal keeps "servants"; Balanced and Readable say "officials", as elsewhere in Samuel and Kings.

source.text: וַיִּקְרָ֤א מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ לְכָל־זִקְנֵ֣י הָאָ֔רֶץ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ דְּעֽוּ־נָ֣א וּרְא֔וּ כִּ֥י רָעָ֖ה זֶ֣ה מְבַקֵּ֑שׁ כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֨ח אֵלַ֜י לְנָשַׁ֤י וּלְבָנַי֙ וּלְכַסְפִּ֣י וְלִזְהָבִ֔י וְלֹ֥א מָנַ֖עְתִּי מִמֶּֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And called [the] king of Israel to all [the] elders of the land and said, Know, please, and see that trouble this [one] [is] seeking; for he sent to me for my wives and for my sons and for my silver and for my gold, and not I withheld from him.

en.L: And the king of Israel called all the elders of the land and said, "Know, please, and see that this [man] is seeking harm; for he sent to me for my wives and for my sons and for my silver and for my gold, and I did not withhold [them] from him."
en.B: Then the king of Israel called in all the elders of the land and told them, "Look and see how this man is out to do us harm! He sent to me for my wives and my {{gender:children|sons}}, my silver and my gold, and I did not refuse him."
en.R: So the king of Israel called together all the leaders of the land. He said, "You can see that this man wants to ruin us. He sent to me and asked for my wives and {{gender:children|sons}}, my silver and gold, and I did not say no to him."

decisions.choice: harm: ruin, not only hard terms
decisions.reason: The word means evil or disaster. Ahab tells the elders that Ben-hadad's new demand shows he is not after tribute but wants to plunder and ruin them.

decisions.choice: the elders of the land: the leading men of the clans and towns
decisions.reason: The elders were heads of families who spoke for the people (8:1; 21:8). Ahab seeks their backing before defying Ben-hadad.

decisions.choice: I did not withhold them: I already agreed to the first demand
alternatives: I have not yet refused him
decisions.reason: Ahab reminds them that he accepted the claim of verse 3 (verse 4). It is the second demand, to search and plunder, that he now puts before them.

decisions.choice: leaders
decisions.reason: Readable says "leaders" for the elders, since their age is not the point but their place in the community.

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

source.text: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ אֵלָ֛יו כָּל־הַזְּקֵנִ֖ים וְכָל־הָעָ֑ם אַל־תִּשְׁמַ֖ע וְל֥וֹא תֹאבֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him all the elders and all the people, Do not listen, and not will you consent.

en.L: And all the elders and all the people said to him, "Do not listen, and do not consent."
en.B: All the elders and all the people told him, "Do not listen to him, and do not give in."
en.R: All the leaders and all the people answered, "Do not listen to him. Do not agree to it."

decisions.choice: do not listen, and do not consent: a firm double refusal
decisions.reason: The first verb is a plain command not to obey; the second, with a stronger negative, says that consenting is out of the question.

decisions.choice: all the people: the people in the besieged city
decisions.reason: Here the people are those shut up in Samaria, who would suffer from a plundering. Their support stands beside the elders' counsel.

decisions.choice: to him
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add whom Ahab is not to listen to: Ben-hadad.

source.text: וַיֹּ֜אמֶר לְמַלְאֲכֵ֣י בֶן־הֲדַ֗ד אִמְר֞וּ לַֽאדֹנִ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ כֹּל֩ אֲשֶׁר־שָׁלַ֨חְתָּ אֶל־עַבְדְּךָ֤ בָרִֽאשֹׁנָה֙ אֶעֱשֶׂ֔ה וְהַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה לֹ֥א אוּכַ֖ל לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת וַיֵּֽלְכוּ֙ הַמַּלְאָכִ֔ים וַיְשִׁבֻ֖הוּ דָּבָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said to [the] messengers of Ben-hadad, Say to my lord the king, All that you sent to your servant at the first I will do, but this thing not I am able to do. And went the messengers and brought him back word.

en.L: And he said to the messengers of Ben-hadad, "Say to my lord the king, 'All that you sent to your servant [for] at the first I will do, but this thing I am not able to do.'" And the messengers went and brought him back word.
en.B: So he told Ben-hadad's messengers, "Tell my lord the king, 'I will do everything you demanded of your servant the first time, but this I cannot do.'" The messengers left and took the answer back to Ben-hadad.
en.R: So Ahab said to Ben-hadad's messengers, "Tell my master the king, 'I will do everything you first asked of your servant. But I cannot do this.'" The messengers left and took his answer back to Ben-hadad.

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "me"
decisions.reason: Speaking of oneself as "your servant" was the courteous way to address a superior (Genesis 18:3; 1 Samuel 20:7-8). Ahab still speaks as Ben-hadad's subject while he refuses the second demand.

decisions.choice: this thing: the demand to search and plunder
decisions.reason: Ahab will keep the terms of verse 3, which he accepted, but not the new demand of verses 5-6.

decisions.choice: brought him back word: reported to Ben-hadad
decisions.reason: "Him" is Ben-hadad, to whom the messengers return.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: All three levels keep "your servant", so the polite form of Ahab's reply is heard.

decisions.choice: to Ben-hadad
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Ben-hadad for "him".

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֵלָיו֙ בֶּן־הֲדַ֔ד וַיֹּ֕אמֶר כֹּֽה־יַעֲשׂ֥וּן לִ֛י אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְכֹ֣ה יוֹסִ֑פוּ אִם־יִשְׂפֹּק֙ עֲפַ֣ר שֹׁמְר֔וֹן לִשְׁעָלִ֕ים לְכָל־הָעָ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּרַגְלָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent to him Ben-hadad and said, Thus may do to me gods and thus may they add, if will suffice [the] dust of Samaria for handfuls for all the people who [are] at my feet.

en.L: And Ben-hadad sent to him and said, "Thus may the gods do to me, and thus may they add, if the dust of Samaria will be enough for handfuls for all the people who [are] at my feet."
en.B: Then Ben-hadad sent him this message: "May the gods deal with me ever so severely if Samaria's dust is enough to give a handful to each of the troops who follow me!"
en.R: Then Ben-hadad sent another message: "May the gods punish me terribly if I leave enough of Samaria for each of my soldiers to carry away a handful of its dust!"

decisions.choice: thus may the gods do to me, and thus may they add: an oath calling down a curse on oneself
decisions.reason: The speaker calls on the gods to punish him if he does not do what he says. Jezebel swears the same way in 19:2 (compare 1 Samuel 3:17). Ben-hadad swears by his own gods; the verb is plural.

decisions.choice: the dust of Samaria will not be enough for handfuls: Samaria will be ground to nothing
decisions.reason: Ben-hadad boasts that his army is so large, and the destruction will be so complete, that the city reduced to dust would not give each of his men a handful.

decisions.choice: the people at my feet: the troops who follow me
decisions.reason: To be "at someone's feet" is to follow him (Judges 4:10; 8:5). Here the people are his army.

decisions.choice: May the gods punish me severely if I leave enough of Samaria ...
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the oath is a threat to destroy Samaria completely, and puts the boast about the dust after it.

decisions.choice: troops (Balanced); soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: The people who follow a king to war are his army.

decisions.choice: Thus may the gods do to me, and thus may they add (Literal); May the gods deal with me ever so severely (Balanced); May the gods punish me terribly (Readable)
decisions.reason: The oath is worded as in 19:2 and 1 Samuel 14:44 at each level.

source.text: וַיַּ֤עַן מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דַּבְּר֔וּ אַל־יִתְהַלֵּ֥ל חֹגֵ֖ר כִּמְפַתֵּֽחַ׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered [the] king of Israel and said, Speak: Not let boast [one] girding like [one] loosening.

en.L: And the king of Israel answered and said, "Tell [him], 'Let not [the one] girding [armor] on boast like [the one] loosening [it].'"
en.B: The king of Israel answered, "Tell him: 'The man buckling his armor on should not brag like the man unbuckling it.'"
en.R: The king of Israel answered, "Tell him this: 'A soldier just putting on his armor should not brag as if he were already taking it off after the battle.'"

decisions.choice: a saying: boast when the battle is over, not before it
decisions.reason: This is a proverb of four Hebrew words. The one girding is a warrior fastening on his belt and weapons before a fight; the one loosening is a warrior unfastening them afterward, when he knows he has won. Ahab answers Ben-hadad's oath with a soldier's proverb: the outcome is not decided yet.

decisions.choice: girding: fastening on the belt that held weapons and armor
decisions.reason: The verb means to bind on a belt or sash. A soldier girded himself with his sword and gear before battle (1 Samuel 17:39; 25:13).

decisions.choice: armor
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not name what is put on and taken off. Literal brackets "armor"; Balanced and Readable supply it, and Readable adds "after the battle" to make the point of the saying plain.

decisions.choice: the saying set as a quotation
decisions.reason: Ahab tells the messengers what to say, so the proverb stands as words quoted within his reply.

source.text: וַיְהִ֗י כִּשְׁמֹ֨עַ֙ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה וְה֥וּא שֹׁתֶ֛ה ה֥וּא וְהַמְּלָכִ֖ים בַּסֻּכּ֑וֹת וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֶל־עֲבָדָיו֙ שִׂ֔ימוּ וַיָּשִׂ֖ימוּ עַל־הָעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, when he heard this word, and he [was] drinking, he and the kings, in the booths, and he said to his servants, Set! And they set against the city.

en.L: And it happened, when he heard this word, while he [was] drinking, he and the kings, in the booths, that he said to his servants, "Set [yourselves]!" And they set [themselves] against the city.
en.B: Ben-hadad heard this reply while he and the kings were drinking in their shelters. He said to his officials, "Take your positions!" So they took up positions against the city.
en.R: When Ben-hadad heard this answer, he and the other kings were drinking in their tents. He told his officers, "Get ready to attack!" So they got ready to attack the city.

decisions.choice: the booths: shelters in the camp
decisions.reason: The word names temporary shelters made of branches or cloth (Genesis 33:17), here in the army's camp. It is also the name of a town, Succoth, in the Jordan valley, and some read "in Succoth" here and in verse 16, but Succoth was far from Samaria.

decisions.choice: Set!: a military command to take up positions
decisions.reason: The verb "set" or "place" has no object. It is a short battle order: set yourselves in position, or set the siege works, against the city.

decisions.choice: drinking: Ben-hadad feasts while his men prepare
decisions.reason: The scene is repeated in verse 16, where Ben-hadad is drunk when Israel attacks. His careless confidence matches his boast in verse 10.

decisions.choice: officials (Balanced); officers (Readable)
decisions.reason: The servants of a king are his officials; here they carry out a military order, so Readable says "officers".

decisions.choice: Ben-hadad
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Ben-hadad for "he".

source.text: וְהִנֵּ֣ה׀נָבִ֣יא אֶחָ֗ד נִגַּשׁ֮ אֶל־אַחְאָ֣ב מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הְֽרָאִ֔יתָ אֵ֛ת כָּל־הֶהָמ֥וֹן הַגָּד֖וֹל הַזֶּ֑ה הִנְנִ֨י נֹתְנ֤וֹ בְיָֽדְךָ֙ הַיּ֔וֹם וְיָדַעְתָּ֖ כִּֽי־אֲנִ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And look, a prophet, one, drew near to Ahab king of Israel and said, Thus says Yahweh, Have you seen all this great multitude? Look, I [am] giving it into your hand today, and you will know that I [am] Yahweh.

en.L: And look, a certain prophet came near to Ahab king of Israel and said, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'Have you seen all this great multitude? Look, I am giving it into your hand today, and you will know that I [am] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.B: Just then a prophet came up to Ahab king of Israel and said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'Do you see this whole huge army? I am handing it over to you today, and then you will know that I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.R: Then a prophet came to Ahab, the king of Israel. He said, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'Do you see this enormous army? Today I will let you defeat it. Then you will know that I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"

decisions.choice: a certain prophet: a prophet who is not named
decisions.reason: The prophet is not Elijah. Even after the killing of the LORD's prophets (18:4, 13), others were still active in Israel, and the LORD sends one of them to Ahab.

decisions.choice: give into your hand: give you victory over
decisions.reason: To give an enemy into someone's hand is to let him defeat it (Judges 7:9).

decisions.choice: you will know that I am Yahweh: the victory will show who the LORD is
decisions.reason: The same words are spoken to Pharaoh and Egypt in the exodus story (Exodus 7:5, 17). The LORD rescues Ahab, who has followed Baal (16:31-33), so that he will know the LORD as God, as the people confessed at Carmel (18:39).

decisions.choice: look (Literal); just then (Balanced)
decisions.reason: The word that draws attention to something new is given as "look" in Literal and as "just then" in Balanced, not the old word "behold".

decisions.choice: I will let you defeat it
decisions.reason: Readable explains "give it into your hand".

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אַחְאָב֙ בְּמִ֔י וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה בְּנַעֲרֵ֖י שָׂרֵ֣י הַמְּדִינ֑וֹת וַיֹּ֛אמֶר מִֽי־יֶאְסֹ֥ר הַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אָֽתָּה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Ahab, By whom? And he said, Thus says Yahweh, By [the] young men of [the] princes of the provinces. And he said, Who will bind the battle? And he said, You.

en.L: And Ahab said, "By whom?" And he said, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'By the young men of the princes of the provinces.'" And he said, "Who will begin the battle?" And he said, "You."
en.B: Ahab asked, "By whom?" He answered, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'By the young men of the provincial officials.'" Ahab asked, "Who will start the battle?" He answered, "You will."
en.R: Ahab asked, "Who will do it?" The prophet answered, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'The young soldiers of the district leaders will do it.'" Then Ahab asked, "Who will start the attack?" The prophet answered, "You will."

decisions.choice: young men: junior fighters
decisions.reason: The word means young men, and is often used of young soldiers or attendants (1 Samuel 14:1; 2 Samuel 2:14). These belong to the officials of the districts, so they are a small band of picked men, not the main army.

decisions.choice: the princes of the provinces: the officials over the districts of the kingdom
decisions.reason: The kingdom was divided into districts, each with its governor (compare 4:7-19). Their young men may have taken refuge in Samaria with them. A band of only 232 (verse 15) makes it plain that the victory will be the LORD's.

decisions.choice: bind the battle: begin the fighting
decisions.reason: The verb means to bind or harness; with "battle" it means to start the fight or join battle (2 Chronicles 13:3).

decisions.choice: princes (Literal); officials (Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The levels follow the wording settled for this word in Samuel and Kings; Readable adds "district" for the provinces.

decisions.choice: The prophet answered; Who will do it?
decisions.reason: Readable names the speakers and spells out Ahab's short question.

source.text: וַיִּפְקֹ֗ד אֶֽת־נַעֲרֵי֙ שָׂרֵ֣י הַמְּדִינ֔וֹת וַיִּהְי֕וּ מָאתַ֖יִם שְׁנַ֣יִם וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֑ים וְאַחֲרֵיהֶ֗ם פָּקַ֧ד אֶת־כָּל־הָעָ֛ם כָּל־בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שִׁבְעַ֥ת אֲלָפִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And he mustered the young men of [the] princes of the provinces, and they were two hundred thirty and two; and after them he mustered all the people, all [the] sons of Israel, seven thousand.

en.L: And he mustered the young men of the princes of the provinces, and they were 232; and after them he mustered all the people, all the sons of Israel, 7,000.
en.B: So Ahab mustered the young men of the provincial officials, 232 of them. After them he mustered all the troops, all the Israelites, 7,000 in all.
en.R: So Ahab called up the young soldiers of the district leaders. There were 232 of them. Then he called up the rest of the army, all the Israelites who were there. There were 7,000 of them.

decisions.choice: all the people, all the sons of Israel: all the fighting men Ahab had
decisions.reason: The "people" here are the army, and "all the sons of Israel" means all the Israelite fighting men on hand in Samaria, not the whole nation.

decisions.choice: seven thousand: the size of the numbers
decisions.reason: The word for "thousand" may also name a military unit; see the note at Numbers 1. The same question applies to the large numbers in verses 29 and 30.

decisions.choice: seven thousand: the same number as in 19:18
decisions.reason: In 19:18 the LORD tells Elijah that he will keep 7,000 in Israel who have not bowed to Baal. The number here may recall that word, but the text does not link the two.

decisions.choice: sons of Israel (Literal); Israelites (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: These are fighting men, so the gender setting used elsewhere for this phrase does not apply. Balanced and Readable say "Israelites".

decisions.choice: troops (Balanced); army (Readable)
decisions.reason: The people mustered for war are the army.

source.text: וַיֵּצְא֖וּ בַּֽצָּהֳרָ֑יִם וּבֶן־הֲדַד֩ שֹׁתֶ֨ה שִׁכּ֜וֹר בַּסֻּכּ֗וֹת ה֧וּא וְהַמְּלָכִ֛ים שְׁלֹשִֽׁים־וּשְׁנַ֥יִם מֶ֖לֶךְ עֹזֵ֥ר אֹתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And they went out at noon, and Ben-hadad [was] drinking drunk in the booths, he and the kings, thirty and two kings helping him.

en.L: And they went out at noon, while Ben-hadad [was] drinking himself drunk in the booths, he and the kings, thirty-two kings helping him.
en.B: They marched out at noon, while Ben-hadad was getting drunk in the shelters with the thirty-two kings who were his allies.
en.R: They marched out at noon. At that time Ben-hadad and the thirty-two kings who had joined him were in their tents, getting drunk.

decisions.choice: at noon: in the heat of the day
decisions.reason: Midday was a time for rest (2 Samuel 4:5). An attack then would catch a careless camp off guard.

decisions.choice: drinking drunk: drinking until he was drunk
decisions.reason: The two words together describe a man well into his drinking, not a single cup (compare 16:9).

decisions.choice: thirty-two kings helping him: his allies
decisions.reason: These are the kings of verse 1, who fought on Ben-hadad's side.

decisions.choice: allies (Balanced); who had joined him (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Helping him" names the kings' part in the war.

decisions.choice: shelters (Balanced); tents (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 12.

source.text: וַיֵּצְא֗וּ נַעֲרֵ֛י שָׂרֵ֥י הַמְּדִינ֖וֹת בָּרִֽאשֹׁנָ֑ה וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח בֶּן־הֲדַ֗ד וַיַּגִּ֤ידוּ לוֹ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר אֲנָשִׁ֕ים יָצְא֖וּ מִשֹּׁמְרֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And went out [the] young men of [the] princes of the provinces at the first; and sent Ben-hadad, and they told him, saying, Men have come out from Samaria.

en.L: And the young men of the princes of the provinces went out first. And Ben-hadad sent [out], and they told him, saying, "Men have come out from Samaria."
en.B: The young men of the provincial officials went out first. Ben-hadad sent out scouts, and they reported to him, "Men are coming out of Samaria."
en.R: The young soldiers of the district leaders led the way. Ben-hadad had sent men to watch, and they told him, "Some men are coming out of Samaria."

decisions.choice: Ben-hadad sent: he sent men to find out
decisions.reason: The verb has no object. Ben-hadad sent someone out, and those he sent brought back word.

decisions.choice: first: the young men lead, and the army follows
decisions.reason: The young men go ahead, as the LORD said (verse 14), and the rest of Ahab's army follows them (verse 19).

decisions.choice: scouts (Balanced); men to watch (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whom Ben-hadad sent; Literal brackets "out".

source.text: וַיֹּ֛אמֶר אִם־לְשָׁל֥וֹם יָצָ֖אוּ תִּפְשׂ֣וּם חַיִּ֑ים וְאִ֧ם לְמִלְחָמָ֛ה יָצָ֖אוּ חַיִּ֥ים תִּפְשֽׂוּם׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, If for peace they have come out, seize them alive; and if for battle they have come out, alive seize them.

en.L: And he said, "If they have come out for peace, seize them alive; and if they have come out for battle, alive seize them."
en.B: He said, "If they have come out to make peace, take them alive. If they have come out to fight, take them alive."
en.R: He said, "Capture them alive, whether they have come out to ask for peace or to fight."

decisions.choice: seize them alive: either way, take them prisoner
decisions.reason: The two halves of the order mirror each other, with the words "alive" and "seize" changing places. Whatever the men intend, Ben-hadad wants them captured, not fought.

decisions.choice: for peace: to ask for terms
decisions.reason: Men coming out of a besieged city might be envoys seeking terms of surrender. Ben-hadad, drunk and sure of himself, does not take them seriously as a threat.

decisions.choice: whether ... or
decisions.reason: Readable puts the two matching halves into one sentence.

source.text: וְאֵ֨לֶּה֙ יָצְא֣וּ מִן־הָעִ֔יר נַעֲרֵ֖י שָׂרֵ֣י הַמְּדִינ֑וֹת וְהַחַ֖יִל אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַחֲרֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And these went out from the city, [the] young men of [the] princes of the provinces, and the army which [was] after them.

en.L: And these went out from the city: the young men of the princes of the provinces, and the army that [was] behind them.
en.B: So these went out from the city: the young men of the provincial officials, and the army behind them.
en.R: The young soldiers of the district leaders marched out of the city, and the rest of the army followed them.

decisions.choice: these went out: the story returns to the Israelites
decisions.reason: After Ben-hadad's order, the narrator turns back to the men leaving Samaria: first the young men, then the 7,000 of verse 15.

decisions.choice: the rest of the army followed them
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that this army is the main force mustered in verse 15.

source.text: וַיַּכּוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ אִישׁ֔וֹ וַיָּנֻ֣סוּ אֲרָ֔ם וַֽיִּרְדְּפֵ֖ם יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּמָּלֵ֗ט בֶּן־הֲדַד֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אֲרָ֔ם עַל־ס֖וּס וּפָרָשִֽׁים׃

records.literal_gloss: And they struck each his man, and fled Aram, and pursued them Israel; and escaped Ben-hadad king of Aram on a horse, and horsemen.

en.L: And they struck each his man, and Aram fled, and Israel pursued them; and Ben-hadad king of Aram escaped on a horse, and horsemen [with him].
en.B: Each of them struck down his man. The Arameans fled, and Israel chased them, but Ben-hadad king of Aram escaped on horseback with some horsemen.
en.R: Each Israelite soldier killed the enemy soldier he fought. The Arameans ran away, and the Israelites chased them. But Ben-hadad, the king of Aram, got away on a horse, along with some of his horsemen.

decisions.choice: struck each his man: each killed the man he met
decisions.reason: The phrase pictures every Israelite fighter overcoming the enemy facing him (compare 2 Samuel 2:16).

decisions.choice: Aram: the Aramean army
decisions.reason: The name of the country stands for its people and its army.

decisions.choice: on a horse, and horsemen: he fled on horseback, with horsemen
decisions.reason: The words are brief. They most likely mean that Ben-hadad escaped riding a horse, with some horsemen who escaped with him.

decisions.choice: the Arameans
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "the Arameans" where "Aram" means the people or the army.

decisions.choice: Each Israelite soldier killed the enemy soldier he fought
decisions.reason: Readable spells out who struck whom.

source.text: וַיֵּצֵא֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיַּ֥ךְ אֶת־הַסּ֖וּס וְאֶת־הָרָ֑כֶב וְהִכָּ֥ה בַאֲרָ֖ם מַכָּ֥ה גְדוֹלָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And went out [the] king of Israel and struck the horse and the chariotry, and struck Aram [with] a great striking.

en.L: And the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and the chariots, and struck Aram [with] a great slaughter.
en.B: The king of Israel went out and attacked the horses and chariots, and inflicted a heavy defeat on the Arameans.
en.R: Then the king of Israel went out and attacked the horses and chariots. He badly defeated the Arameans.

decisions.choice: struck with a great striking: a heavy defeat
decisions.reason: The verb and the noun come from the same root: the Arameans were struck down in great numbers (Joshua 10:10; Judges 11:33).

decisions.choice: struck the horses and the chariots: attacked the chariot force
decisions.reason: The horses and chariots were the strongest part of Ben-hadad's army (verse 1). Ahab now joins the fight and attacks them.

decisions.choice: the Arameans
decisions.reason: As in verse 20.

source.text: וַיִּגַּ֤שׁ הַנָּבִיא֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ לֵ֣ךְ הִתְחַזַּ֔ק וְדַ֥ע וּרְאֵ֖ה אֵ֣ת אֲשֶֽׁר־תַּעֲשֶׂ֑ה כִּ֚י לִתְשׁוּבַ֣ת הַשָּׁנָ֔ה מֶ֥לֶךְ אֲרָ֖ם עֹלֶ֥ה עָלֶֽיךָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And drew near the prophet to [the] king of Israel and said to him, Go, strengthen yourself, and know and see what you will do, for at [the] return of the year [the] king of Aram [will be] coming up against you.

en.L: And the prophet came near to the king of Israel and said to him, "Go, strengthen yourself, and know and see what you will do, for at the return of the year the king of Aram [will be] coming up against you."
en.B: Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and said to him, "Go and build up your strength. Think carefully about what you must do, because in the spring the king of Aram will march against you."
en.R: Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and said, "Go and make your army stronger. Think about what you need to do. The king of Aram is going to attack you again next spring."

decisions.choice: the return of the year: the spring
decisions.reason: The year was counted as turning in the spring, the season when kings went out to war after the winter rains (2 Samuel 11:1).

decisions.choice: strengthen yourself: make yourself strong for war
decisions.reason: The verb means to take courage and to build up one's strength. Here it points to preparing the army and the defenses.

decisions.choice: know and see: consider carefully
decisions.reason: The pair of verbs calls for careful thought before acting (1 Samuel 25:17).

decisions.choice: make your army stronger; again
decisions.reason: Readable says what the strengthening is for and adds "again", since the king of Aram has just been driven off.

decisions.choice: in the spring (Balanced); next spring (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the season meant by "the return of the year".

source.text: וְעַבְדֵ֨י מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֜ם אָמְר֣וּ אֵלָ֗יו אֱלֹהֵ֤י הָרִים֙ אֱלֹ֣הֵיהֶ֔ם עַל־כֵּ֖ן חָזְק֣וּ מִמֶּ֑נּוּ וְאוּלָ֗ם נִלָּחֵ֤ם אִתָּם֙ בַּמִּישׁ֔וֹר אִם־לֹ֥א נֶחֱזַ֖ק מֵהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] servants of [the] king of Aram said to him, Gods of hills [are] their gods; therefore they were stronger than us. But let us fight with them on the plain; if not we will be stronger than they.

en.L: And the servants of the king of Aram said to him, "Their gods [are] gods of hills; that is why they were stronger than we. But let us fight against them on the level ground; surely we will be stronger than they.
en.B: Meanwhile the officials of the king of Aram advised him, "Their gods are gods of the hills, and so they were too strong for us. But let us fight them on the plain, and we will certainly be stronger than they are.
en.R: Meanwhile, the officials of the king of Aram gave him this advice: "Israel's gods are gods of the hills. That is why the Israelites were too strong for us. But let us fight them on flat ground. Then we will surely beat them.

decisions.choice: their gods are gods of the hills: the Arameans think Israel's God rules only the high ground
alternatives: Their God is a god of the hills
decisions.reason: In the world around Israel each god was thought to rule a land or a kind of place. Samaria stands on a hill, and Israel's worship was linked with mountains (Sinai, Carmel). The Arameans conclude that on level ground the god of Israel would be powerless. The word for God has a plural form and is used for the one God of Israel as well as for many gods; in the Arameans' mouths it may mean either. Verse 28 quotes them as speaking of the LORD as one god.

decisions.choice: if not we will be stronger: surely we will be stronger
decisions.reason: "If not" is the form of an oath: "may something happen to us if we are not stronger". It makes a firm claim.

decisions.choice: the plain: level ground
decisions.reason: The word means flat land, where chariots could move freely, unlike the hills around Samaria.

decisions.choice: servants (Literal); officials (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The servants of a king are his officials. Literal keeps "servants"; Balanced and Readable say "officials", as elsewhere in Samuel and Kings.

decisions.choice: Meanwhile; Israel's gods
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable mark the change of scene to the Aramean camp, and Readable says whose gods are meant.

source.text: וְאֶת־הַדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּ֖ה עֲשֵׂ֑ה הָסֵ֤ר הַמְּלָכִים֙ אִ֣ישׁ מִמְּקֹמ֔וֹ וְשִׂ֥ים פַּח֖וֹת תַּחְתֵּיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And this thing do: remove the kings, each from his place, and put governors in their place.

en.L: And do this thing: remove the kings, each from his place, and put governors in their place.
en.B: And do this: remove each of the kings from his post, and put governors in their place.
en.R: Do this: take the kings out of command, and put your own officers in charge instead.

decisions.choice: governors: officials appointed by the king
decisions.reason: The word names officers set over a region or a force by the king (10:15). Unlike the allied kings, who led their own men, governors would owe everything to Ben-hadad and obey him.

decisions.choice: remove the kings: one command instead of many
decisions.reason: The officials blame the defeat partly on a divided command of thirty-two kings (verse 16). One army under officers answerable to Ben-hadad would fight as one.

decisions.choice: put your own officers in charge
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the governors were: men chosen by Ben-hadad himself.

source.text: וְאַתָּ֣ה תִֽמְנֶה־לְךָ֣׀חַ֡יִל כַּחַיִל֩ הַנֹּפֵ֨ל מֵאוֹתָ֜ךְ וְס֣וּס כַּסּ֣וּס׀וְרֶ֣כֶב כָּרֶ֗כֶב וְנִֽלָּחֲמָ֤ה אוֹתָם֙ בַּמִּישׁ֔וֹר אִם־לֹ֥א נֶחֱזַ֖ק מֵהֶ֑ם וַיִּשְׁמַ֥ע לְקֹלָ֖ם וַיַּ֥עַשׂ כֵּֽן׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And you, you will count for yourself an army like the army that fell from you, and horse for horse and chariotry for chariotry, and let us fight with them on the plain; if not we will be stronger than they. And he listened to their voice and did so.

en.L: And you, number for yourself an army like the army that fell from you, horse for horse and chariot for chariot, and let us fight against them on the level ground; surely we will be stronger than they." And he listened to their voice and did so.
en.B: Then raise an army for yourself like the army you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot, and let us fight them on the plain. We will certainly be stronger than they are." He took their advice and did so.
en.R: Then build up an army like the one you lost. Get a horse for every horse you lost and a chariot for every chariot. Then we will fight them on flat ground, and we will surely beat them." The king did what they said.

decisions.choice: count for yourself an army: raise an army
decisions.reason: The verb means to count or assign. Here it means to gather and enroll an army as large as the one before.

decisions.choice: the army that fell from you: the army you lost
decisions.reason: The army fell in battle, and so Ben-hadad lost it.

decisions.choice: listened to their voice: followed their advice
decisions.reason: To listen to someone's voice is to do what they say.

decisions.choice: surely we will be stronger
decisions.reason: As in verse 23.

decisions.choice: Get a horse for every horse you lost
decisions.reason: Readable spells out "horse for horse".

source.text: וַֽיְהִי֙ לִתְשׁוּבַ֣ת הַשָּׁנָ֔ה וַיִּפְקֹ֥ד בֶּן־הֲדַ֖ד אֶת־אֲרָ֑ם וַיַּ֣עַל אֲפֵ֔קָה לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was at [the] return of the year, and mustered Ben-hadad Aram and went up to Aphek for battle with Israel.

en.L: And it happened at the return of the year that Ben-hadad mustered Aram and went up to Aphek for battle with Israel.
en.B: In the spring Ben-hadad mustered the Arameans and marched up to Aphek to fight against Israel.
en.R: The next spring, Ben-hadad called up the Aramean army and went to the town of Aphek to fight against Israel.

decisions.choice: Aphek: probably the town east of the Sea of Galilee
decisions.reason: Several towns bore this name (Joshua 12:18; 1 Samuel 4:1; 29:1). This one is most likely the Aphek on the road from Damascus, east of the Sea of Galilee, near level ground suited to chariots, as the Arameans wanted (verse 23). The site is not certain.

decisions.choice: the return of the year: the spring
decisions.reason: As in verse 22. The prophet's warning comes true.

decisions.choice: the Arameans (Balanced); the Aramean army (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 20.

source.text: וּבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל הָתְפָּקְדוּ֙ וְכָלְכְּל֔וּ וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ לִקְרָאתָ֑ם וַיַּחֲנ֨וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל נֶגְדָּ֗ם כִּשְׁנֵי֙ חֲשִׂפֵ֣י עִזִּ֔ים וַאֲרָ֖ם מִלְא֥וּ אֶת־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] sons of Israel were mustered and were provisioned and went to meet them; and camped [the] sons of Israel before them like two little flocks of goats, and Aram filled the land.

en.L: And the sons of Israel were mustered and supplied, and they went to meet them; and the sons of Israel camped opposite them like two little flocks of goats, while Aram filled the land.
en.B: The Israelites were mustered and given supplies, and they went out to meet them. The Israelites camped facing them like two little flocks of goats, while the Arameans filled the whole land.
en.R: The Israelites also gathered their army, got their supplies, and went out to fight them. The Israelite camp facing the Arameans looked like two little flocks of goats, but the Arameans filled the whole land.

decisions.choice: supplied: given food and provisions
decisions.reason: The verb means to provide for or feed (4:7; 17:4). The army was given what it needed for the campaign.

decisions.choice: little flocks: small, separated flocks
decisions.reason: The word is found only here. From the context it names a small flock, perhaps one cut off from the main herd. The sense is not certain.

decisions.choice: like two little flocks of goats: few and exposed
decisions.reason: The picture sets Israel's small camp, perhaps in two divisions, against the Arameans who filled the land. The odds look hopeless.

decisions.choice: sons of Israel (Literal); Israelites (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.

source.text: וַיִּגַּ֞שׁ אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים וַיֹּאמֶר֮ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וַיֹּ֜אמֶר כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה יַ֠עַן אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָמְר֤וּ אֲרָם֙ אֱלֹהֵ֤י הָרִים֙ יְהוָ֔ה וְלֹֽא־אֱלֹהֵ֥י עֲמָקִ֖ים ה֑וּא וְ֠נָתַתִּי אֶת־כָּל־הֶהָמ֨וֹן הַגָּ֤דוֹל הַזֶּה֙ בְּיָדֶ֔ךָ וִֽידַעְתֶּ֖ם כִּֽי־אֲנִ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And drew near [the] man of God and said to [the] king of Israel and said, Thus says Yahweh, Because that said Aram, A god of hills [is] Yahweh, and not a god of valleys [is] he, and I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you will know that I [am] Yahweh.

en.L: And the man of God came near and spoke to the king of Israel and said, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'Because Aram has said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} [is] a god of hills, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} [is] not a god of valleys," I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you will know that I [am] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.B: Then the man of God came to the king of Israel and said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'Because the Arameans have said that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is a god of the hills and not a god of the valleys, I will hand this whole huge army over to you, and you will know that I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.R: Then the man of God came and spoke to the king of Israel: "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'The Arameans say that I, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, am a god of the hills and not a god of the valleys. Because they said that, I will let you defeat this enormous army. Then you will know that I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"

decisions.choice: a god of hills and not of valleys: the LORD answers the Arameans' claim
decisions.reason: The Arameans have said that Israel's god is limited to one kind of ground (verse 23). The LORD will prove them wrong by giving Israel victory on the plain. He is not a local god but the God who rules everywhere.

decisions.choice: the man of God: a prophet
decisions.reason: "Man of God" is another name for a prophet (13:1; 17:18). The text does not say whether he is the prophet of verses 13 and 22 or another.

decisions.choice: you will know that I am Yahweh
decisions.reason: As in verse 13. The verb here is plural, so the promise is for Israel as well as for the king.

decisions.choice: valleys: low ground
decisions.reason: The word means valleys or lowlands. It stands for the level ground of verse 23, the opposite of the hills.

decisions.choice: the Arameans
decisions.reason: As in verse 20. Balanced and Readable give the Arameans' words as reported speech.

source.text: וַֽיַּחֲנ֧וּ אֵ֦לֶּה נֹ֥כַח אֵ֖לֶּה שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֑ים וַיְהִ֣י׀בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י וַתִּקְרַב֙ הַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וַיַּכּ֨וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֧ל אֶת־אֲרָ֛ם מֵאָה־אֶ֥לֶף רַגְלִ֖י בְּי֥וֹם אֶחָֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And camped these opposite these seven days; and it was on the day the seventh, and drew near the battle, and struck [the] sons of Israel Aram, one hundred thousand foot soldiers in day one.

en.L: And they camped, these opposite these, seven days; and it happened on the seventh day that the battle drew near, and the sons of Israel struck Aram, 100,000 foot soldiers in one day.
en.B: For seven days the two armies camped opposite each other. On the seventh day the battle was joined, and the Israelites struck down 100,000 Aramean foot soldiers in a single day.
en.R: The two armies camped facing each other for seven days. On the seventh day the battle began. In that one day the Israelites killed 100,000 Aramean soldiers who fought on foot.

decisions.choice: the battle drew near: the fighting began
decisions.reason: The battle "coming near" means the armies closed and fought (Judges 20:23 uses a similar picture).

decisions.choice: foot soldiers: men who fought on foot
decisions.reason: The word sets the infantry apart from the horses and chariots.

decisions.choice: one hundred thousand: the size of the number
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.

decisions.choice: sons of Israel (Literal); Israelites (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.

decisions.choice: the two armies ... each other
decisions.reason: "These opposite these" means the two armies facing each other.

source.text: וַיָּנֻ֨סוּ הַנּוֹתָרִ֥ים׀אֲפֵקָה֮ אֶל־הָעִיר֒ וַתִּפֹּל֙ הַחוֹמָ֔ה עַל־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְשִׁבְעָ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף אִ֖ישׁ הַנּוֹתָרִ֑ים וּבֶן־הֲדַ֣ד נָ֔ס וַיָּבֹ֥א אֶל־הָעִ֖יר חֶ֥דֶר בְּחָֽדֶר׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And fled the remaining [ones] to Aphek, into the city, and fell the wall on twenty and seven thousand men, the remaining [ones]; and Ben-hadad fled and came into the city, a room in a room.

en.L: And the rest fled to Aphek, into the city, and the wall fell on 27,000 men who were left. And Ben-hadad fled and came into the city, [into] a room within a room.
en.B: The rest fled into the town of Aphek, and the wall fell on 27,000 of the men who were left. Ben-hadad also fled into the town and hid in an inner room.
en.R: The rest of the Arameans ran away to the town of Aphek. There the city wall fell on 27,000 of the men who were left. Ben-hadad also ran into the town and hid in a room deep inside a house.

decisions.choice: a room in a room: an inner room
decisions.reason: The phrase means a room inside another room, a hidden place (22:25; 2 Kings 9:2). Ben-hadad, who boasted in verse 10, is now in hiding.

decisions.choice: the wall fell: no cause is given
decisions.reason: The narrator does not say why the wall fell. Coming after the LORD's promise in verse 28, the disaster is part of the victory he gave.

decisions.choice: twenty-seven thousand: the size of the number
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.

decisions.choice: hid
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "hid", which is the point of fleeing into an inner room.

source.text: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵלָיו֮ עֲבָדָיו֒ הִנֵּֽה־נָ֣א שָׁמַ֔עְנוּ כִּ֗י מַלְכֵי֙ בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּֽי־מַלְכֵ֥י חֶ֖סֶד הֵ֑ם נָשִׂ֣ימָה נָּא֩ שַׂקִּ֨ים בְּמָתְנֵ֜ינוּ וַחֲבָלִ֣ים בְּרֹאשֵׁ֗נוּ וְנֵצֵא֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אוּלַ֖י יְחַיֶּ֥ה אֶת־נַפְשֶֽׁךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him his servants, Look, please, we have heard that [the] kings of [the] house of Israel, that kings of steadfast love [are] they. Let us put, please, sackcloth on our loins and ropes on our heads and go out to [the] king of Israel; perhaps he will keep alive your soul.

en.L: And his servants said to him, "Look, now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are kings of steadfast love. Please let us put sackcloth on our loins and ropes on our heads, and go out to the king of Israel; perhaps he will spare your life."
en.B: His officials said to him, "Listen, we have heard that the kings of Israel's royal house are kings who show faithful love. Let us tie sackcloth around our waists and put ropes on our heads, and go out to Israel's king. Perhaps he will spare your life."
en.R: His officials said to him, "We have heard that the kings of Israel show faithful love. Let us wear rough sackcloth around our waists and put ropes on our heads. Then let us go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will let you live."

decisions.choice: kings of steadfast love: kings known for keeping faith and showing mercy
decisions.reason: The word means loyal, faithful kindness, often within a covenant or treaty. Ben-hadad's men hope that the kings of Israel will be true to a beaten enemy who submits and treat him mercifully.

decisions.choice: sackcloth on our loins and ropes on our heads: signs of surrender
decisions.reason: Sackcloth was coarse cloth worn in mourning and humbling (21:27; Genesis 37:34). Ropes on the head are not found elsewhere; they most likely showed that the men gave themselves up as captives, to be led as the victor wished.

decisions.choice: the house of Israel: the kingdom of Israel and its kings
decisions.reason: The Arameans speak of the kings of Israel as a line of rulers they have dealt with before.

decisions.choice: keep alive your soul: spare your life
decisions.reason: "Soul" here is the person's life.

decisions.choice: kings who show faithful love (Balanced); show faithful love (Readable)
decisions.reason: *Chesed* is "steadfast love" at Literal and "faithful love" at Balanced and Readable throughout, and is kept here too; the note (m1) says that here it means keeping faith with a beaten enemy and sparing him.

decisions.choice: loins (Literal); waists (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "Loins" is the part of the body where a belt or wrap was tied; Balanced and Readable say "waists".

source.text: וַיַּחְגְּרוּ֩ שַׂקִּ֨ים בְּמָתְנֵיהֶ֜ם וַחֲבָלִ֣ים בְּרָאשֵׁיהֶ֗ם וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ עַבְדְּךָ֧ בֶן־הֲדַ֛ד אָמַ֖ר תְּחִֽי־נָ֣א נַפְשִׁ֑י וַיֹּ֛אמֶר הַעוֹדֶ֥נּוּ חַ֖י אָחִ֥י הֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: And they girded sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads and came to [the] king of Israel and said, Your servant Ben-hadad says, Let live, please, my soul. And he said, [Is] he still alive? My brother [is] he.

en.L: And they girded sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads, and came to the king of Israel and said, "Your servant Ben-hadad says, 'Please let my soul live.'" And he said, "Is he still alive? He [is] my brother."
en.B: So they tied sackcloth around their waists and ropes on their heads, came before the king of Israel, and told him, "Your servant Ben-hadad pleads, 'Please spare my life.'" Ahab replied, "Is he still alive? He is my brother."
en.R: So they tied sackcloth around their waists and put ropes on their heads. They came to Israel's king and said, "Ben-hadad, your servant, begs you, 'Please let me live.'" The king answered, "Is he still alive? He is my brother."

decisions.choice: your servant Ben-hadad: the roles are reversed
decisions.reason: Ben-hadad, who demanded that Ahab call himself "your servant" (verses 4, 9), now uses the same humble words of himself.

decisions.choice: my brother: an equal and a partner
decisions.reason: Kings who made treaties called each other "brother" (9:13). Ahab does not treat Ben-hadad as a beaten enemy but as an equal king with whom he can make terms.

decisions.choice: let my soul live: let me live
decisions.reason: As in verse 31, "soul" means the person's life.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: All three levels keep "your servant", as in verse 9.

decisions.choice: put ropes on their heads; Ahab replied
decisions.reason: The verb "girded" covers both the sackcloth and the ropes; Readable gives the ropes their own verb. Balanced names Ahab as the speaker.

source.text: וְהָאֲנָשִׁים֩ יְנַחֲשׁ֨וּ וַֽיְמַהֲר֜וּ וַיַּחְלְט֣וּ הֲמִמֶּ֗נּוּ וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ אָחִ֣יךָ בֶן־הֲדַ֔ד וַיֹּ֖אמֶר בֹּ֣אוּ קָחֻ֑הוּ וַיֵּצֵ֤א אֵלָיו֙ בֶּן־הֲדַ֔ד וַֽיַּעֲלֵ֖הוּ עַל־הַמֶּרְכָּבָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And the men were watching for an omen, and hurried and caught [it]: whether from him? And they said, Your brother Ben-hadad. And he said, Go, bring him. And came out to him Ben-hadad, and he made him come up on the chariot.

en.L: And the men took it as an omen, and they quickly caught [it] from him, and said, "Your brother Ben-hadad!" And he said, "Go, bring him." And Ben-hadad came out to him, and he had him come up on the chariot.
en.B: The men took this as a good sign and quickly seized on his word, saying, "Yes, your brother Ben-hadad!" He said, "Go and bring him." When Ben-hadad came out to him, Ahab had him come up into his chariot.
en.R: The men were watching for a sign of hope, and they quickly took up the word Ahab had used. They said, "Yes, your brother Ben-hadad!" Ahab said, "Go and get him." When Ben-hadad came out, Ahab invited him up into his chariot.

decisions.choice: watching for an omen: looking for a sign of how things would go
decisions.reason: The verb is used of reading signs or omens (Genesis 44:5). Here the men take Ahab's word "brother" as a sign that he will be kind.

decisions.choice: caught it from him: took up his word at once
alternatives: caught it up to see whether he meant it
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is unusual here: the word for "from him" has a question marker attached, perhaps "whether it was from him", that is, whether he meant it. The sense is that they seized on Ahab's word and repeated it back to hold him to it.

decisions.choice: up on the chariot: a mark of honor
decisions.reason: Inviting another man into one's chariot showed favor and friendship (2 Kings 10:15-16). The beaten king rides as Ahab's equal.

decisions.choice: Yes
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "yes" to show that the men are repeating and confirming Ahab's word.

decisions.choice: Ahab
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Ahab for "he".

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֡יו הֶעָרִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר־לָֽקַח־אָבִי֩ מֵאֵ֨ת אָבִ֜יךָ אָשִׁ֗יב וְ֠חוּצוֹת תָּשִׂ֨ים לְךָ֤ בְדַמֶּ֨שֶׂק֙ כַּאֲשֶׁר־שָׂ֤ם אָבִי֙ בְּשֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן וַאֲנִ֖י בַּבְּרִ֣ית אֲשַׁלְּחֶ֑ךָּ וַיִּכְרָת־ל֥וֹ בְרִ֖ית וַֽיְשַׁלְּחֵֽהוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And he said to him, The cities which took my father from with your father I will return, and streets you will set for yourself in Damascus, as set my father in Samaria. And I, with a covenant I will send you away. And he cut with him a covenant and sent him away.

en.L: And he said to him, "The cities that my father took from your father I will return, and you may set up streets for yourself in Damascus, as my father set up in Samaria." [And Ahab said,] "And I, with a covenant I will send you away." And he made a covenant with him and sent him away.
en.B: Ben-hadad said to him, "I will give back the cities my father took from your father, and you may set up your own market streets in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria." Ahab said, "On the terms of a treaty I will set you free." So he made a treaty with him and let him go.
en.R: Ben-hadad told Ahab, "I will give back the towns my father took from your father. You may have your own trading streets in Damascus, as my father had in Samaria." Ahab answered, "I will let you go free if we make an agreement." So Ahab made an agreement with him and let him go.

decisions.choice: streets: trading quarters for merchants
decisions.reason: The word means streets or open places. Here it most likely means market streets where merchants of the other kingdom could trade with special rights, a valuable privilege for the king who held them.

decisions.choice: and I, with a covenant I will send you away: Ahab now speaks
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not say that the speaker changes, but "I will send you away" can only be said by Ahab, who holds Ben-hadad's life in his hand. He accepts the offer and sets the terms.

decisions.choice: my father ... your father: the kings before them
decisions.reason: "Father" may mean the reigning king's father or simply his predecessor. An earlier Ben-hadad took towns from Israel in Baasha's time (15:20). The text does not tell of a war between Omri and Aram.

decisions.choice: covenant: a treaty between kings
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for God's covenant with Israel, but between kings it means a formal treaty with terms and oaths (5:26; 15:19).

decisions.choice: And Ahab said
decisions.reason: The change of speaker is not marked in the Hebrew. Literal brackets the words; Balanced and Readable add them.

decisions.choice: treaty (Balanced); agreement (Readable)
decisions.reason: Between kings the word means a treaty. Literal keeps "covenant".

source.text: וְאִ֨ישׁ אֶחָ֜ד מִבְּנֵ֣י הַנְּבִיאִ֗ים אָמַ֧ר אֶל־רֵעֵ֛הוּ בִּדְבַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה הַכֵּ֣ינִי נָ֑א וַיְמָאֵ֥ן הָאִ֖ישׁ לְהַכֹּתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And a man, one, of [the] sons of the prophets said to his companion by [the] word of Yahweh, Strike me, please. And refused the man to strike him.

en.L: And a certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his companion by the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Strike me, please." But the man refused to strike him.
en.B: By the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} one of the company of prophets said to his companion, "Please strike me." But the man would not strike him.
en.R: One man from a group of prophets, obeying a command from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, said to his friend, "Please hit me." But the man refused.

decisions.choice: the sons of the prophets: a community of prophets
decisions.reason: "Sons of the prophets" means members of a group of prophets who lived and worked together, often under a leading prophet (2 Kings 2:3, 5; 4:38; 6:1). It does not mean that their fathers were prophets.

decisions.choice: by the word of Yahweh: at the LORD's command
decisions.reason: The prophet does not ask on his own whim; the LORD told him to (13:1-2, 9). That is why the refusal is serious (verse 36).

decisions.choice: strike me: hit me so as to wound me
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to hit or to kill. Verse 37 shows that the prophet wanted a wound, to make his disguise believable.

decisions.choice: sons of the prophets (Literal); company of prophets (Balanced); group of prophets (Readable)
decisions.reason: The levels follow the wording settled for this phrase in Samuel and Kings.

decisions.choice: hit
decisions.reason: Readable says "hit", since the man is to be wounded, not killed.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ יַ֚עַן אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־שָׁמַ֨עְתָּ֙ בְּק֣וֹל יְהוָ֔ה הִנְּךָ֤ הוֹלֵךְ֙ מֵֽאִתִּ֔י וְהִכְּךָ֖ הָאַרְיֵ֑ה וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ מֵֽאֶצְל֔וֹ וַיִּמְצָאֵ֥הוּ הָאַרְיֵ֖ה וַיַּכֵּֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said to him, Because that not you listened to [the] voice of Yahweh, look, you [are] going from with me, and will strike you the lion. And he went from beside him, and found him the lion and struck him.

en.L: And he said to him, "Because you have not listened to the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, look, you [are] going from me, and the lion will strike you." And he went from beside him, and the lion found him and struck him.
en.B: So he said to him, "Because you have not obeyed {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, as soon as you leave me a lion will kill you." And when he had left him, a lion found him and killed him.
en.R: Then the prophet said, "You did not obey {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. So when you leave me, a lion will kill you." The man left, and a lion met him and killed him.

decisions.choice: the lion: the same judgment as in chapter 13
decisions.reason: In 13:24-26 a man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD was killed by a lion on the road. The same fate shows that refusing the LORD's word, even in a small matter, is serious.

decisions.choice: the lion: a lion, the one that will meet him
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "the lion", pointing ahead to the particular lion of the story, not to one already mentioned.

decisions.choice: not listened to the voice of Yahweh: refusing the LORD's command
decisions.reason: The companion's refusal may have looked kind, but he refused a command given by the LORD's word. The story points ahead to Ahab, who will be judged for sparing the man the LORD had condemned (verse 42).

decisions.choice: obeyed
decisions.reason: "Listened to the voice of" means obeyed.

decisions.choice: kill
decisions.reason: Here the verb "strike" means to strike dead.

source.text: וַיִּמְצָא֙ אִ֣ישׁ אַחֵ֔ר וַיֹּ֖אמֶר הַכֵּ֣ינִי נָ֑א וַיַּכֵּ֥הוּ הָאִ֖ישׁ הַכֵּ֥ה וּפָצֹֽעַ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he found a man, another, and said, Strike me, please. And struck him the man, striking and wounding.

en.L: And he found another man and said, "Strike me, please." And the man struck him, striking and wounding [him].
en.B: He found another man and said to him, "Please strike me." This man struck him and left him wounded.
en.R: Then the prophet found another man and said, "Please hit me." So the man hit him hard and wounded him.

decisions.choice: striking and wounding: he struck him so that he was wounded
decisions.reason: Two verb forms follow the main verb to show the result: the blow drew blood or bruised him.

decisions.choice: the wound: part of the disguise
decisions.reason: A wounded man coming from the battle would pass for a soldier (verse 39).

decisions.choice: hit him hard
decisions.reason: As in verse 35, Readable says "hit"; "hard" brings out the strong verb forms.

source.text: וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ הַנָּבִ֔יא וַיַּעֲמֹ֥ד לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ עַל־הַדָּ֑רֶךְ וַיִּתְחַפֵּ֥שׂ בָּאֲפֵ֖ר עַל־עֵינָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And went the prophet and stood for the king on the road, and he disguised himself with the bandage over his eyes.

en.L: And the prophet went and stood [waiting] for the king by the road, and he disguised himself with a bandage over his eyes.
en.B: Then the prophet went and waited for the king by the road. He disguised himself with a bandage over his eyes.
en.R: Then the prophet went and waited beside the road for the king to come by. He covered his eyes with a bandage so that no one would know who he was.

decisions.choice: bandage: a cloth tied over the eyes
decisions.reason: The word is found only here and in verse 41. From the context it is a cloth or headband tied over the eyes, such as a wounded man might wear.

decisions.choice: disguised himself: so that the king would not know him as a prophet
decisions.reason: The prophet must look like an ordinary soldier, so that Ahab will judge the case without knowing that it is about him (verse 41).

decisions.choice: so that no one would know who he was
decisions.reason: Readable says why he covered his eyes.

source.text: וַיְהִ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ עֹבֵ֔ר וְה֖וּא צָעַ֣ק אֶל־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיֹּ֜אמֶר עַבְדְּךָ֣׀יָצָ֣א בְקֶֽרֶב־הַמִּלְחָמָ֗ה וְהִנֵּֽה־אִ֨ישׁ סָ֜ר וַיָּבֵ֧א אֵלַ֣י אִ֗ישׁ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ שְׁמֹר֙ אֶת־הָאִ֣ישׁ הַזֶּ֔ה אִם־הִפָּקֵד֙ יִפָּקֵ֔ד וְהָיְתָ֤ה נַפְשְׁךָ֙ תַּ֣חַת נַפְשׁ֔וֹ א֥וֹ כִכַּר־כֶּ֖סֶף תִּשְׁקֽוֹל׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, the king [was] passing by, and he cried out to the king and said, Your servant went out into [the] midst of the battle, and look, a man turned aside and brought to me a man and said, Guard this man; if being missing he is missing, and will be your life in place of his life, or a talent of silver you will weigh out.

en.L: And it happened, as the king was passing by, that he cried out to the king and said, "Your servant went out into the midst of the battle, and look, a man turned aside and brought a man to me and said, 'Guard this man. If he is missing at all, then your life will be in place of his life, or you will weigh out a talent of silver.'
en.B: As the king passed by, the prophet called out to him, "Your servant went out into the thick of the battle, and suddenly a man turned aside and brought me a prisoner. He said, 'Guard this man. If he is ever missing, it will be your life for his life, or else you must pay {{units:about 75 pounds of silver|a talent of silver}}.'
en.R: When the king passed by, the prophet shouted to him, "Your servant went into the middle of the battle. Then a soldier came over to me with a prisoner. He said, 'Guard this man. If he gets away, you will die in his place, or you will have to pay {{units:about 75 pounds of silver|a talent of silver}}.'

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "me"
decisions.reason: As in verse 9. The prophet speaks as a common soldier asking the king for justice.

decisions.choice: your life in place of his life: you will die if he escapes
decisions.reason: The guard would pay with his own life. Verse 42 turns the same words on Ahab.

decisions.choice: a talent of silver: a huge sum
decisions.reason: A talent was about 75 pounds. No common soldier could pay so much, so in practice the penalty was death. Silver was weighed out, not counted as coins.

decisions.choice: if being missing he is missing: if he is missing at all
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis: if the man is in any way missing.

decisions.choice: {{units:about 75 pounds of silver|a talent of silver}}
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the weight in modern measure, with the original unit as the alternative; Literal keeps "talent".

decisions.choice: prisoner
decisions.reason: The man brought to him is a captive from the battle, as the order to guard him shows.

source.text: וַיְהִ֣י עַבְדְּךָ֗ עֹשֵׂ֥ה הֵ֛נָּה וָהֵ֖נָּה וְה֣וּא אֵינֶ֑נּוּ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֧יו מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל כֵּ֥ן מִשְׁפָּטֶ֖ךָ אַתָּ֥ה חָרָֽצְתָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, your servant [was] doing here and there, and he, he [was] not. And said to him [the] king of Israel, So [is] your judgment; you, you have decided [it].

en.L: And it happened, [while] your servant [was] busy here and there, he [was] gone." And the king of Israel said to him, "So [is] your judgment; you yourself have decided [it]."
en.B: But while your servant was busy with this and that, the man was gone." The king of Israel said to him, "That is your sentence. You have pronounced it yourself."
en.R: But while I was busy with other things, the man got away." The king of Israel said to him, "Then that is your punishment. You have said so yourself."

decisions.choice: doing here and there: busy with this and that
decisions.reason: The phrase pictures a man busy with other things, not paying attention to his prisoner.

decisions.choice: your judgment: the sentence on you
decisions.reason: The word means a legal decision. The king rules that the soldier must bear the penalty he agreed to.

decisions.choice: you have decided it: the king judges himself
decisions.reason: Like Nathan's story to David (2 Samuel 12:1-7) and the woman of Tekoa's story (2 Samuel 14:4-11), the prophet's case leads the king to pass sentence, and then the sentence is turned on him (verse 42).

decisions.choice: I
decisions.reason: Readable says "I" for "your servant" here, since the polite form was given in verse 39.

source.text: וַיְמַהֵ֕ר וַיָּ֨סַר֙ אֶת־הָ֣אֲפֵ֔ר מֵעֲלֵ֖י עֵינָ֑יו וַיַּכֵּ֤ר אֹתוֹ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּ֥י מֵֽהַנְּבִאִ֖ים הֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: And he hurried and removed the bandage from over his eyes, and recognized him [the] king of Israel, that of the prophets [was] he.

en.L: And he quickly removed the bandage from over his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him, that he [was] one of the prophets.
en.B: Then the man quickly took the bandage off his eyes, and the king of Israel knew him for one of the prophets.
en.R: Then the prophet quickly pulled the bandage off his eyes. The king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.

decisions.choice: recognized him as one of the prophets
decisions.reason: The king may have known the man by sight, or known him as a prophet by some mark. The text says only that once the bandage was off, the king saw that he was a prophet.

decisions.choice: the bandage
decisions.reason: As in verse 38.

decisions.choice: the man (Balanced); the prophet (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֗יו כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה יַ֛עַן שִׁלַּ֥חְתָּ אֶת־אִישׁ־חֶרְמִ֖י מִיָּ֑ד וְהָיְתָ֤ה נַפְשְׁךָ֙ תַּ֣חַת נַפְשׁ֔וֹ וְעַמְּךָ֖ תַּ֥חַת עַמּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said to him, Thus says Yahweh, Because you have let go the man of my devoting from [your] hand, and will be your life in place of his life, and your people in place of his people.

en.L: And he said to him, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'Because you have let go from [your] hand the man of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} devoting, your life will be in place of his life, and your people in place of his people.'"
en.B: The prophet said to him, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'Because you have let go the man I had devoted to destruction, your life will go for his life, and your people for his people.'"
en.R: The prophet told him, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'I had decided that this man must be destroyed completely, as given over to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. But you let him go. So you will die in his place, and your people will die in place of his people.'"

decisions.choice: the man of my devoting: the man I had devoted to destruction
decisions.reason: The word names what is given over to the LORD to be destroyed and may not be spared or kept (Joshua 6:17; 7:1). The LORD had given Ben-hadad into Ahab's hand (verse 28); he was not Ahab's to set free.

decisions.choice: letting go the devoted man: as Saul spared Agag
decisions.reason: Saul spared Agag king of Amalek, whom the LORD had devoted to destruction, and lost his kingdom (1 Samuel 15:8-9, 23).

decisions.choice: your life for his life: Ahab will die, and his people will suffer
decisions.reason: The sentence Ahab passed on the soldier (verse 40) falls on him. Ahab later dies fighting the Arameans (22:34-37), and Israel suffers at their hands.

decisions.choice: destroyed completely, as given over to me
decisions.reason: Readable explains the term in the way settled for it, with the LORD speaking of himself.

source.text: וַיֵּ֧לֶךְ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל עַל־בֵּית֖וֹ סַ֣ר וְזָעֵ֑ף וַיָּבֹ֖א שֹׁמְרֽוֹנָה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And went [the] king of Israel to his house sullen and angry, and came to Samaria.

en.L: And the king of Israel went to his house sullen and angry, and came to Samaria.
en.B: The king of Israel set off for his palace, sullen and angry, and came to Samaria.
en.R: The king of Israel went home to Samaria, upset and angry.

decisions.choice: sullen and angry: resentful and bitter
decisions.reason: The two words describe a man in a bad temper, sulking rather than repenting. The same words describe Ahab in 21:4.

decisions.choice: his house: his palace in Samaria
decisions.reason: His house is the royal palace; the verse ends with his arrival in the capital.

decisions.choice: went home to Samaria
decisions.reason: Readable joins going home and coming to Samaria into one phrase, and says "upset" for "sullen".
